## What I was trying to do

Get a shared home for the group's AI experiments online, without spending a month on it
and without a stack that only I can maintain. The constraint that mattered most: a
colleague who has never used git should be able to add their project.

## How it works

The site is [Quarto](https://quarto.org), which renders Markdown into a static website,
deployed by GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages. Every project on the site is either a Markdown
file or four lines of YAML, so contributing never requires running anything locally.

The work happened in three passes rather than one. First a design spec, which forced the
decisions that are expensive to change later: what a contribution *is*, who reviews it,
where it is hosted. Then an implementation plan broken into tasks small enough to verify
one at a time. Only then the code.

## What worked and what did not

Writing the spec first was the whole game. The agent pushed back on sequencing the
contributor tooling before the content schema was frozen, which would have meant building
it twice.

What did not work was assuming. Two claims about how Quarto listings behave, mixing local
pages with external links in one grid, and excluding a template file from that grid, both
turned out to be true, but only after testing them. A third assumption, about which CSS
class Quarto emits for a custom field, turned out to be wrong and would have shipped as
silently dead styling. The habit worth copying is asking for the check rather than the
confident answer.
